The Nazi jurists, including press chief Du Prel and Minister Frank, were completely baffled when they read it. They called it “liberal.”

Fortunately for me, Hitler himself never saw it. He would have sensed what it meant: to take the tried-and-tested trick of legality out of his hands and force him into legal responsibility. He would once again have staged one of his fits of rage against the jurists. There is only one way for the philosopher or jurist to deal with the ruler: take him at his word. That too is a form of Taking.
Compare the story in Funck-Brentano, Le Roi (1907):
“Your Majesty will decide the case personally.”

The editors of the Rheinischer Merkur—Roegele—deleted my name from an article by Walter Warnach about Spain and Calvo Serer. So I still have a guardian angel after all. He guides the hand of these people who strike my name out. They intend evil, and the guardian angel turns it into good.
I would have been very embarrassed if my name had appeared in that article.
At the end of May I wrote to Peter Schneider to acknowledge receipt of his book:
“for me, as the object of this vivisection—or better: this Arcanoscopy.”
I thought the coinage “Arcanoscopy”—an inspection of my secret—was especially witty. But neither Rüdiger Altmann nor Johannes Groß reacted to it.
Apparently my contacts and my antennae are failing.
What am I still doing in the world? Do you see how the lightning falls over there?
A delightful conversation with George Schwab about homo homini homo—man is man to man.
In what concrete situation is that true?
On a bus, surely, homo homini homo applies.
Man is man to man, and neither God nor wolf.
But in a philosophical discussion, homo homini homo means nothing other than:
Man is an alibi for man. For whom?
An alibi for the God and an alibi for the Wolf.

You use the wrong intoxicant. You take opium instead of drinking wine. Religion becomes the opium of the people when the laity has its wine taken away. Naturally they have to run to foreign gods once they start taking foreign intoxicants.
The priest has stolen away the wine. We have a great deal to make up for.

The surest way to abolish the priesthood is the universal priesthood. If all laypeople are supposed to become priests, then all priests are more likely to become laypeople than all laypeople are to become priests. The level at which the two sides finally meet will be the lowest and most comfortable one: universal lay status. Not universal priesthood. That is the path of democracy.
The democratic way of life. It is the road forced upon us by the logic of concepts of this kind.
The final result of a jurist’s existence:
I do not want to have power.
But I want even less to be in the right.
So my heartfelt condolences on your constitutional state!

The steel bells that call a person to church in this country—those are no longer my bells. Everything else follows by itself: those are no longer my songs; those are no longer my wines; not even my schnapps anymore. It is Coca-Cola-coalition music.
In Heidelberg I quoted to Carl-Joachim Friedrich the line:
Those bells were never yours, and they are no longer mine.
At that very moment the bells for Vespers were ringing.
In America you rarely hear church bells ringing.
In Wiesbaden, at Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, we laughed at Adorno’s revealing remark about Hegel’s “grandiose peasant cunning.”
In that remark you can see a cloven hoof that may turn into a boomerang and, as Hans Barion added, strike an Achilles heel.
How amusing these self-revelations of the great revealers are.

How disgusting the whole philosophy of work then becomes: with its servant undermining the master, its serva padrona—the servant who becomes mistress, its successful private tutor, and all the social climbers who marry aristocratic girls and eventually create in Darwinism their grand myths of the ambitious survivor who compensates for his physical weakness through intelligence.
So that was the European nineteenth century.
Perhaps I will live to see its end.
How magnificent, by contrast, was Hans Freyer’s reply to Arnold Gehlen’s birthday speech:
What we have gained is: progress in the mode of failure.
The infiltrator writes sociology. And Samuel Pepys crawls into his diary.
When I was talking with A. Kojève about the falsification of the sacrament and complained about the withholding of the wine, he replied:
The layman has too much blood anyway.
At that moment I noticed that he was a cleric and I was a layman. And yet no Iron Curtain fell between us. Nor did the speaking grille of a confessional.
In Wiesbaden, in his speech for Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, Arnold Gehlen declared: we are passing from one age, the age of history, into another—the age of sociology.
The age of history is over.

According to Kojève’s interpretation, Hegel had already said the same thing. But Hegel did not yet know what Gehlen knows: that the age—one presumably must no longer say time—of sociology is now beginning.
And how pleasant to hear and believe.
The end of time has arrived.
History was never the ground of happiness.
That, presumably, will be the ground of happiness.

The real explosive force of the atomic bomb strikes the very concept of the human being. It drives homo homini homo out of its comfortable hiding place and blows apart the threefold neutrality of this threefold tautology.
Human beings drop atomic bombs made by human beings onto the heads of other human beings.
That is the reality of homo homini homo. Here human beings are completely among themselves. So where is the true human being?
And what becomes of the other person, who by consequence is no longer a true human being?
I really ought to start thinking about a Song of the Seventy-Year-Old, an antistrophe to my Song of the Sixty-Year-Old.
Listen and suffer! Listen and suffer?
I listen and hear nothing anymore. I suffer and feel nothing anymore. What am I still doing in the world? Waiting until the atomic bomb is hurled?
Spare yourself the death of an insect that threatens from Nobel Prize clouds.
Leave this establishment before the brothel owner throws you out and has his police arrest you as an enemy of the constitutional state.

Or rather with the cheerfulness of an all-knowing old man who knows that he has passed beyond the line and nothing can happen to him anymore, because neither a declaration of enmity nor the decoration of some order can still reach him?
Perhaps you should sing of progress?
Progress in the consciousness of freedom, with Hegel.
Progress in the consciousness of the distinction between friend and enemy.
Progress in the consciousness of defeat.
Progress from taking land to taking sea, and from there to taking industry,
Progress in the methods used to liquidate whoever disturbs the cleansing.
